column2: On the authority of the Mother of the Believers, Umm ʿAbdillāh ʿĀʾishah (may Allah be pleased with her), who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

“Whoever introduces into this matter of ours what is not part of it, it is rejected.” Reported by al-Bukhārī and Muslim. In a narration of Muslim: “Whoever does a deed that is not in accordance with our matter, it is rejected.”

This hadith is a foundational principle for weighing outward deeds: they count only if they conform to the Sharīʿah, just as the hadith “Actions are only by intentions” is a foundational principle for inward deeds,
[showing] that every deed by which one seeks nearness to Allah must be done sincerely for Allah and is judged by its intention.

If acts of worship such as wuḍūʾ, the bath for major ritual impurity, the prayer and so on are done contrary to the Sharīʿah, they are rejected and do not count; and what is taken under an invalid contract must be returned to its owner and does not become one's property.

Evidence of this is the story of the hired worker, where the Prophet ﷺ said to his father: “As for the slave-girl and the sheep, they are returned to you.” Reported by al-Bukhārī (2695) and Muslim (1697).

The hadith also shows that whoever invents an innovation that has no basis in the Sharīʿah, it is rejected, and its originator deserves the threatened punishment. The Prophet ﷺ said concerning Madīnah:
“Whoever introduces into it an innovation or shelters an innovator, upon him is the curse of Allah, the angels and all the people.” Reported by al-Bukhārī (1870) and Muslim (1366).
The second narration, recorded by Muslim, is more general than the narration in the two Ṣaḥīḥs,
because it includes whoever practises an innovation, whether he is the one who introduced it or someone preceded in introducing it who follows the one who did.

The meaning of his word in the hadith, radd (“rejected”), is “thrown back upon him”. It is a verbal noun used in the sense of a passive participle, like khalq in the sense of makhlūq (“created”) and naskh in the sense of mansūkh (“abrogated”). The meaning is: it is void and does not count.

The hadith does not include things of public benefit that serve to preserve the religion or lead to understanding and knowing it, such as compiling the Qurʾān into written copies (maṣāḥif), recording the sciences of language and grammar, and so on.

By its unrestricted wording, the hadith shows that every deed contrary to the Sharīʿah is rejected, even if the doer's intention was good. Evidence of this is the story of the Companion who slaughtered his sacrifice before the ʿĪd prayer,
to whom the Prophet ﷺ said: “Your sheep is just a sheep for meat.” Reported by al-Bukhārī (955) and Muslim (1961).

By its explicit wording, this hadith shows that every deed not in accordance with the command of the Lawgiver is rejected, and by its implied meaning, that every deed in accordance with His command is not rejected.
The meaning is that whoever's deeds proceed under the rulings of the Sharīʿah and conform to them, they are accepted; and whoever's deeds fall outside that, they are rejected.
The prohibition of innovating in the religion.
A deed based on an innovation is rejected and thrown back on the one who does it.
A prohibition entails invalidity.

When a righteous deed is done in a way that is not prescribed, such as voluntary prayer without a reason at a time when prayer is forbidden, or fasting on the day of ʿĪd, and the like, it is void and does not count.
The judgement of a judge does not change the inner reality of a matter,
because he said: “that is not in accordance with our matter”.
An invalid settlement is void, and what is taken under it must be returned, as in the hadith of the hired worker.
